title: Robust CZ gate against flux line memory
abstract: High-fidelity CZ gates are central to superconducting quantum processors, but implementations based on flux tuning are still sensitive to pulse distortion. Conventional predistortion, typically used for an isolated gate, can recover the desired flux at the chip but it fails if the flux line memory exists, causing the fidelity of repeated CZ gates to drop rapidly. To address this issue, we model the flux line distortion as the dynamics of a stateful classical actuator coupled to a quantum system. Using a first-order Dyson expansion, we derive the error generators induced by variations in the initial flux-line state. We then design a robust CZ gate by optimizing the flux pulse to suppress these generators and minimize the residual flux line state at the gate exit. A one-pole flux line model shows the expected first-order robustness plateau. For a more practical three-pole model, the optimized CZ pulse achieves $F_{\mathrm{avg}}=99.998\%$, suppresses all first-order error generators, and brings the residual flux line state close to zero. With no additional waiting time between gates, our robust pulse achieves $F_{\mathrm{avg}}=99.97\%$ for the complete ten-gate sequence and reduces the sequence infidelity by a factor of about $2.3\times10^{3}$ relative to the baseline under the same predistortion protocol. These results show that explicitly accounting for flux line memory maintains high-fidelity CZ operation across repeated gate sequences and addresses a key limitation of conventional predistortion.
summary: This paper tackles the critical issue of flux line memory degrading gate fidelity in superconducting quantum computers. The authors develop a robust control scheme by modeling the flux line as a stateful actuator and optimizing the control pulse to suppress memory-induced errors. They demonstrate that combining memory robustness and state-closing conditions yields near-perfect fidelity over long gate sequences.
main_problem: The primary challenge is designing high-fidelity Controlled-Z (CZ) gates for superconducting quantum processors that remain robust against flux line memory effects accumulated from previous gate operations.
main_result: By explicitly optimizing the flux pulse to suppress first-order error generators and minimize residual flux, the authors achieved a sequence fidelity of 99.97% over ten gates, significantly outperforming baseline protocols.
method: The authors used a first-order Dyson expansion to derive error generators based on the initial state of the flux line actuator. They then optimized the flux pulse to satisfy two conditions: memory robustness at the gate entrance and zero residual state at the gate exit.
model_or_system: The system involves a superconducting quantum processor (QCQ) coupled to a flux line modeled as a classical, stateful dynamical actuator with memory. The Hamiltonian depends on the applied flux, which is determined by the actuator's state.
key_observables: Average fidelity ($F_{avg}$), first-order error generators ($G_\ell$), and the residual flux line state at the gate exit.
important_parameters: The number of poles in the flux line model (one-pole vs. three-pole), and the sequence length (ten gates).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes a one-way coupling (neglecting backaction) and relies on a finite-dimensional linear model for the actuator dynamics.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the comparison of optimized pulses (memory-robust vs. state-closing vs. combined) showing superior fidelity retention over multiple gates, and diagrams detail the coupling between the quantum system and the stateful actuator.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical model involving the QCQ and the stateful flux actuator. It then develops the error analysis using Dyson expansion to derive necessary conditions for robustness (memory robustness and state closing). Finally, it presents the optimization results using a three-pole model to demonstrate the superior performance of the combined robust pulse.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, mathematically rigorous framework for mitigating systematic errors (memory effects) in superconducting quantum hardware, directly addressing a major bottleneck in scaling quantum processors.
